one_liner: Small multithreaded C directory walker on raw getdents64 that prints every path; beats GNU find and fd on a synthetic tree.
what_it_does: A command-line tool, dent [start_dir] [num_threads], that recursively prints every path under a directory, one per line, in no particular order. It has no filters, no stat, no sorting and no options beyond the thread count (default 10); pattern matching is left to a downstream grep. About 270 lines of C (dent.c, main.c, dent.h); the Makefile also builds a static binary and a dent.so, but there is no documented library API.
how_it_is_fast: Worker threads (pthreads) pop directory paths from a mutex/condvar work queue, read each directory with the raw getdents64 syscall into a 256 KiB thread-local buffer, and recurse into children whose d_type is DT_DIR without ever calling stat. Output is built in a 256 KiB thread-local buffer and written with one fwrite per flush. The speedup over GNU find comes mostly from parallelism (dent's system time, 1.82 s, is over 3x its 0.56 s wall time) plus skipping per-entry libc/fts overhead.
when_to_use: Dumping the full path list of a large tree (hundreds of thousands to millions of entries) on Linux, on a local filesystem that fills in d_type
Feeding a path list to grep or another tool when you do not need find's predicates, ordering or metadata
As a short, readable reference for a parallel getdents64 walker you can adapt into your own C/C++ code (MIT license)
when_not_to_use: Filesystems that return DT_UNKNOWN in d_type (some NFS, older XFS, reiserfs and FUSE setups): dent never stats, so it silently does not descend into those directories
Any use that needs find/fd features: name or type filters, depth limits, ignore files, -exec, stat-based predicates, stable output order
Pipelines that expect clean text paths: entry names are printed with up to 7 trailing NUL padding bytes (see gotchas), which is why the README's grep example needs -a
Long-lived production use: single burst of commits in October 2024, no tests of output correctness against find, code written with ChatGPT per the README

integration.thread_safety: not applicable as a program; list_directory uses static thread-local buffers, so it is not reentrant within one thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — equivalent to a bare 'find DIR' listing (same set of paths, unordered, with NUL padding bytes), nothing more

gotchas: Name length is computed as d_reclen - offsetof(d_name) - 1, but d_reclen is padded to 8 bytes, so each printed name carries 0-7 trailing NUL bytes before the newline. Directory recursion still works (strdup stops at the first NUL), but the output is not byte-identical to find's and needs grep -a; the benchmarked output was this padded form (read from dent.c).

The committed benchmark_scenario.c (DEPTH 4, BREADTH 32) does not produce the README's 765,200-entry tree: it creates 1,082,400 directories and 1,082,400 unique files (the file loop sits inside the directory loop, rewriting the same 32 files 32 times), and its printed counter would read 35,719,200. The tree that was timed is therefore not reproducible from the repo as-is (computed from the source).

README says MAX_CONCURRENT_THREADS in dirlist.h defaults to 1000, but no such file or macro exists; the actual default is 10 threads from main.c, and the README's 'executable named dirlist' is really dent.
README says the project is 'provided as-is without any warranty' but the repo root has an MIT LICENSE (Copyright 2024 roy reznik); open() failures (permissions) are printed with perror and skipped.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick dent only when you want the smallest possible parallel getdents64 walker to copy and you control the filesystem; bfs is the catalogued choice for a find-compatible, maintained traversal tool, and lsr covers single-directory ls -l listing rather than recursive walks.
verified_claims_summary: First-party hyperfine (3 warmups, 10 runs) on a synthetic tree the README says holds 765,200 entries, with warm caches implied: dent 563.9 ms vs GNU find 3.178 s (5.64x) and fdfind -HI 1.633 s (2.90x); piping to grep for one name was 6.01x faster than find -iregex and 1.60x faster than fd. Built with gcc -O3 per the Makefile; CPU, core count, filesystem and kernel are not stated, and dent and fd ran multithreaded while find is single-threaded.
status_note: Stale since 2024-10-03 (ten commits over two days, 18 stars, one closed issue), MIT-licensed and small enough to vendor, but fix the NUL-padding name length before relying on its output.
